questions.question: What is distributed caching?

options.text: Caching on a single powerful server with high memory
Spreading cache data across multiple nodes for scalability and availability
Distributing cache configuration to end users
Caching data at the client browser level

questions.explanation: Distributed caching spreads data across multiple cache nodes. This provides horizontal scalability (more nodes = more capacity), fault tolerance (node failure doesn't lose all data), and can reduce latency by placing data closer to consumers. Twitter uses distributed caching to handle 500M+ tweets daily; Facebook's Memcached cluster handles billions of requests per second.

questions.question: Which are popular distributed caching solutions? (Choose all that apply)

options.text: Redis Cluster
Memcached
Apache Ignite
PostgreSQL

questions.explanation: Redis Cluster, Memcached, and Apache Ignite are distributed caching solutions. PostgreSQL is a relational database—while it has query caching, it's not a distributed cache. Other examples include Hazelcast, Ehcache, and AWS ElastiCache. Each has different tradeoffs: Redis offers rich data structures, Memcached is simpler but multi-threaded, Ignite provides SQL queries on cached data.

questions.question: How does consistent hashing help in distributed caching?

options.text: It encrypts cache data for security
It minimizes data redistribution when cache nodes are added or removed
It compresses cache entries to save memory
It ensures all nodes have identical data

questions.explanation: Consistent hashing maps keys to nodes such that adding/removing a node only affects ~1/N of keys (where N is node count). Without it, simple modulo hashing would invalidate most of the cache when nodes change. Discord uses consistent hashing for their message cache; Amazon's Dynamo popularized the technique. It's essential for elastic scaling without cache stampedes.

questions.question: A distributed cache has 5 nodes. One node fails. What happens to its data?

options.text: All cache data across all nodes is invalidated
Data on that node is lost; requests for those keys become cache misses
Data automatically migrates to surviving nodes
The entire cache cluster stops accepting requests

questions.explanation: Without replication, data on the failed node is lost—those keys become cache misses until re-cached from the source of truth. With replication (Redis Cluster replicas), surviving replicas can serve the data. This is why caches should be treated as ephemeral—your system must handle cache misses gracefully. Netflix designs all services to survive complete cache failure.

questions.question: What is cache replication in distributed systems?

options.text: Copying cache application code to multiple servers
Storing copies of cache data on multiple nodes for fault tolerance
Replicating cache configuration across environments
Duplicating cache requests for load testing

questions.explanation: Cache replication stores data copies on multiple nodes. If one fails, replicas serve requests. Redis Cluster supports replica nodes that automatically promote on master failure. The tradeoff: more memory usage and write overhead, but higher availability. For critical data like session state, replication prevents user-facing errors during node failures.

questions.question: What is the difference between Redis and Memcached for distributed caching?

options.text: They are functionally identical with different APIs
Redis supports data structures and persistence; Memcached is simpler key-value only
Memcached is always faster than Redis
Redis doesn't support clustering or replication

questions.explanation: Redis offers rich data structures (lists, sets, sorted sets, hashes), persistence options, pub/sub, Lua scripting, and transactions. Memcached is simpler key-value storage but multi-threaded (Redis is single-threaded per shard). Instagram uses Redis for complex data; Pinterest uses Memcached for simple caching. Choose based on feature needs—Memcached for simple caching at massive scale, Redis for richer functionality.

questions.question: How should cache clients handle a cache node failure?

options.text: Crash and restart the application
Retry with exponential backoff, fall back to database
Wait indefinitely for the node to recover
Delete all local application data

questions.explanation: Clients should handle cache failures gracefully: retry briefly for transient issues, then fall back to the database. Cache is an optimization, not a requirement—your system must work without it. Circuit breakers can prevent cascading failures if the cache is completely down. Stripe's systems are designed so cache failures cause latency increases, not outages.

questions.question: True or False: In a distributed cache, all nodes must have identical data.

options.text: True - consistency requires all nodes to be synchronized
False - distributed caches typically partition data across nodes

questions.explanation: Distributed caches typically partition (shard) data—each node holds a subset of keys. Only with full replication would all nodes have identical data, which limits scalability (can't exceed single node's memory). Redis Cluster partitions data across shards; each shard may have replicas, but different shards hold different keys. This enables horizontal scaling beyond single-machine limits.

questions.question: What is 'cache coherence' in distributed caching?

options.text: Cache entries being well-organized and indexed
Ensuring all cache nodes have consistent view of data
Cache performance optimization through compression
Security protocol for cache access control

questions.explanation: Cache coherence ensures that when data is updated, all caches reflect the change consistently. In distributed systems, this is challenging due to network delays and partial failures. Strategies include invalidation broadcasts (delete stale entries), versioning (detect stale reads), and TTL-based expiration (eventual consistency). Facebook's cache invalidation system processes millions of invalidations per second.

questions.question: A microservices architecture has services in multiple regions. How should distributed caching be designed?

options.text: Single global cache cluster for consistency
Regional cache clusters with cross-region replication for shared data
No caching in multi-region deployments
Cache only in the primary region

questions.explanation: Regional caches provide low latency (cache near the service). Cross-region replication or invalidation keeps shared data consistent. A global cache adds latency (cross-region round trips). Netflix uses regional caches with eventual consistency; Slack replicates critical cache data across regions. Design depends on consistency requirements—user sessions might need strong consistency, while product catalogs can be eventually consistent.

questions.question: What is 'hot key' problem in distributed caching?

options.text: Cache keys being too long and consuming memory
One key receiving disproportionate traffic, overloading its node
Cache entries expiring too quickly under load
Keys containing sensitive data requiring encryption

questions.explanation: Hot keys (e.g., viral tweet, celebrity profile, flash sale item) concentrate traffic on one node, creating a bottleneck while other nodes sit idle. Solutions: local caching (each app server caches hot keys), key replication across multiple nodes, or splitting hot keys into sub-keys (user:123:0, user:123:1). Twitter faced this with viral tweets; Instagram with celebrity posts.

questions.question: Which factors affect distributed cache performance? (Choose all that apply)

options.text: Network latency between app and cache
Serialization/deserialization overhead
Cache node memory and CPU
Geographic location of the development team

questions.explanation: Network latency affects round-trip time (same-AZ vs cross-AZ matters). Serialization adds CPU overhead—use efficient formats like Protocol Buffers or MessagePack instead of JSON. Node resources limit throughput and storage capacity. Development team location has no impact on runtime performance. Optimizing all three factors is why companies like Discord achieve sub-millisecond cache latencies.
